opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the main thing that's lacking is any real sense of the collective, of the social. The framing in Silicon Valley tends to be very individualistic and, frankly, a bit narcissistic. The goal is to build a single superintelligent entity, a brain in a box, that will think like us, only better, and then somehow solve all our problems. That's science fiction. It's a fine thing to dream about, but it's not a sound engineering goal, and I don't think it's what we actually need.

If you look at what has really transformed human life, it hasn't been one brilliant individual. It's been systems: markets, supply chains, transportation networks, the financial system, medicine as an institution. These are collectives of many agents with different preferences, different information, and different incentives, interacting under scarcity and uncertainty. Intelligence, in a meaningful sense, lives at that level. A market can bring food into a city like Paris every single day, reliably, without any single planner understanding the whole thing. That's an intelligent system, and nobody is trying to make it "conscious."

So when I hear people talk about AGI, I ask: what problem are you solving, and for whom? Where's the economics? Where are the incentives? Who bears the risk, who gets the value? Machine learning by itself is mostly pattern recognition and prediction, and it's very good at that. But once you deploy these systems into the world, you have to think about mechanism design, about game theory, about uncertainty quantification, about the fact that the data comes from people who have their own interests. Those are the questions of statistics, economics, and engineering combined, and they get almost no airtime in the hype cycle.

There's also a kind of anthropomorphism that I find unhelpful. We talk about these models as if they understand, as if they want things, and that pulls the conversation toward fear or worship, when it should be about building reliable, trustworthy infrastructure, the way chemical engineering or civil engineering emerged as disciplines. We don't ask whether a bridge is intelligent. We ask whether it's safe, whether it serves people, whether it was built on sound principles.

So my critique isn't that the technology isn't impressive. It is. It's that the goals are framed around imitating a human mind rather than around creating systems that make human collectives work better: that connect producers and consumers, that create new markets, that give people more agency rather than less. That's the version of this field I'd like to see us aim for.

r001.rationale: The response says Silicon Valley’s framing lacks a collective social focus and asks what problem is being solved and for whom, calling the superintelligence goal an unsound engineering objective.

r002.rationale: It describes the goal as building a brain-like entity that thinks like humans “only better” and then “somehow” solves all problems, identifying the assumption that a more capable human-like system will produce broad benefits.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that the framing is almost entirely about building a single intelligent entity. The goal is stated as "artificial intelligence," and what people mean by that is a kind of imitation of a human, a machine that thinks, that reasons, that's autonomous, that we eventually hand things over to. And I think that's the wrong goal. It's an old goal, a 1950s goal, and it has a certain romance to it, but it's not what's actually been happening, and it's not what we actually need.

What's been happening over the last couple of decades is that we've built large-scale systems that make predictions, that recommend, that route, that learn from data. Those are engineering achievements, but they're not intelligence in the sense that word normally carries. They're pattern recognition at scale. And when the Valley wraps that in the language of intelligence, of AGI, of machines that are about to surpass us, it does two things that I find unfortunate. It overstates what the systems are, and it understates what's really hard.

What's really hard is not the single agent. It's the collective. It's many agents, many people, many systems, all interacting, with scarce resources, with different information, with different goals, with uncertainty everywhere. That's an economics problem as much as a computer science problem. Markets are a form of intelligence. A healthcare system is a form of intelligence, or it should be. A supply chain is. And those systems don't work because one node is brilliant. They work, when they work, because of how information flows, how incentives are aligned, how decisions get made under uncertainty with partial knowledge.

So when I look at the research agenda coming out of the big labs, I see a lot of effort on making one model bigger and more fluent, and very little on the question of how you build a system that creates value for the people in it. The social welfare question, basically. Who benefits? Does the person whose data trained the system get anything back? Does the recommendation you receive reflect your interests or the platform's? Those aren't side questions. They're the engineering questions, if you think of the engineering discipline as something like what civil engineering or chemical engineering became. Those fields didn't just pursue "artificial buildings" or "artificial chemistry." They built principled disciplines around safety, around reliability, around human needs. We haven't built that yet for data and decisions, and the AGI framing actively distracts from it.

There's also a humility issue. The people I admire most in this field, going back to Shannon and Wiener and the early statisticians, were pretty careful about not claiming they'd captured thought. They were building tools for inference, for communication, for control. The current framing has lost that modesty. It talks about intelligence as if it's a quantity you can scale up by adding parameters, and about human-level as if that's a well-defined threshold. I don't think either of those is true, and I think a lot of the public confusion and a lot of the hype cycle follows directly from that confusion in the research community itself.

So, lacking: a focus on the collective rather than the individual, a focus on welfare and incentives rather than capability for its own sake, and a kind of intellectual humility about what we've actually built. The exciting part is that those are solvable problems, they just require bringing in economics, statistics, and a fair amount of social science alongside the computing.

r001.rationale: It says the research agenda lacks a focus on creating value for people and asks who benefits, explicitly identifying the missing societal objective.

r002.rationale: It criticizes scaling models and treating intelligence as a quantity, but does not identify an assumption about more powerful brain-inspired computation automatically producing beneficial outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think the goals are often framed too narrowly around imitating human intelligence. Can we recognize an object, understand a sentence, beat a person at a game? Those are interesting problems, but they don’t by themselves tell us how to build systems that are useful to people.

Think about a transportation system or a healthcare system. You have many people making decisions, with different information and different interests. The problem isn’t simply to put a very smart predictor in the middle. It’s to figure out how decisions interact, how uncertainty is handled, and what incentives the system creates. Economics and statistics become just as important as computer science.

I’d like to see more of an engineering perspective: what principles let us build these systems reliably, at scale, with meaningful benefits for the people participating in them? The aspiration to create something humanlike can distract us from that much larger task.

r001.rationale: It criticizes goals centered on humanlike tasks as too narrow and calls for systems designed to provide meaningful benefits to people, giving transportation and healthcare as societal examples.

r002.rationale: It does not mention brain-inspired computation or the assumption that increasing its power automatically leads to beneficial outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the framing is too often about building an entity that is intelligent, as if intelligence were a property we could isolate inside a box. Can it recognize objects? Can it use language? Can it beat a human at some task? Those are interesting questions, but they’re a rather narrow foundation for an engineering discipline.

What I’d like to see is more attention to systems involving many people, each with their own information, goals, and incentives. If you’re building a medical system, for example, the problem isn’t simply to produce a diagnosis. It’s to help patients, doctors, and hospitals make better decisions together, under uncertainty and with limited resources.

That brings economics, statistics, and computer science into the same conversation. How does information flow? Who has an incentive to provide good information? Who bears the cost when the system makes a mistake? Those questions are central to whether the technology actually works for people.

Silicon Valley tends to reach for the image of an artificial human. I find the prospect of building better ways for humans to cooperate much more compelling.

r001.rationale: The response says Silicon Valley’s focus on isolated intelligence and task performance is too narrow, and calls for building systems that help people make better decisions together.

r002.rationale: It criticizes the image of an artificial human, but does not mention brain-inspired computation or the assumption that making it more powerful will automatically be beneficial.
